analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance plans to cover addiction treatment on equal terms with other medical care.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan substance-abuse treatment parity bill with 61 cosponsors never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred group health plans and individual insurance from putting harsher limits and higher cost-sharing on substance abuse treatment — detox, rehab, outpatient counseling — than on other medical care. Insurers could still choose whether to offer the benefit at all, and small employers and plans whose costs rose 1% or more were exempt. The bill was introduced in May 2003, sent to three House committees, and never came up for a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families with job-based insurance, and people buying individual coverage, whose plans already include substance abuse treatment. Under current rules, plans often cap rehab stays, limit outpatient visits, and charge high deductibles for addiction care while covering heart surgery or cancer treatment far more generously. Parity would have made those caps and cost-sharing match the plan's rules for other medical care, so someone needing detox or residential treatment would face the same access their plan gives for any other illness.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with substance use disorders and their families

how_it_helps.text: Plans could not impose day or visit limits, deductibles, coinsurance, or annual/lifetime dollar caps on substance abuse treatment unless the same limits applied to medical and surgical benefits [S3].
Covered services would include inpatient detoxification, non-hospital residential treatment, outpatient counseling and relapse prevention, and prevention services [S3].
The rules would also apply to individual-market insurance, not just employer plans, and would not override state laws offering stronger protections [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor health plans and the workers covered by them, through somewhat higher premiums as substance abuse treatment became as available and affordable as other care; insurers would absorb richer benefit obligations and lost one of their main cost-control tools.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and insurers, through higher premiums

drawbacks.text: The bill did not require any plan to offer substance abuse treatment benefits at all, so a plan could drop the benefit rather than cover it on par with medical care [S3].
Employers with 2 to 50 employees were exempt entirely, excluding many workers at small businesses, and any plan could opt out if parity raised its costs by 1% or more [S3].
Employers and unions warned-style cost objection: richer addiction benefits would raise premiums, a real cost to businesses and to workers whose wages reflect benefit costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Parity for addiction treatment is a widely supported idea — the same principle became federal law for mental health and substance use in 2008 — because untreated addiction is costly to families, employers, and public budgets. This version was deliberately modest to limit premium increases: it exempted small employers and let plans escape the 1%-cost rule, but those same escape hatches, plus the option to drop the benefit entirely, meant many people the bill was written for would not have been protected. A fairer version would have covered more plans and required the benefit rather than merely regulating it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees and then to subcommittees, none of which ever reported it out, so it never reached the House floor and expired when Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Ramstad (R-MN) introduced the bill on May 22, 2003, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means Committees [S1][S5].
In June 2003 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee (twice) and the Education and the Workforce Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee [S5].
The bill drew 61 cosponsors — 53 Democrats, 7 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but no committee ever acted on it and no vote was ever scheduled [S4][S5].
The 108th Congress ended January 3, 2005, and the bill died without further action [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and employers that would have faced higher premiums and richer benefit obligations were better off because the bill never got a vote. People with substance use disorders who needed their plans to cover detox and rehab on equal terms gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers spared parity costs

for.name: Rep. Jim Ramstad
for.what_they_did: Introduced the parity bill and recruited 61 cosponsors

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never reported it out

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee and its Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the June 2003 subcommittee referral

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan backing from the start: a Republican sponsor with 7 Republican, 53 Democratic, and 1 Independent cosponsors — so partisan division did not stop it; inaction in committee did.

industries.note: Parity would have barred insurers from using day limits, visit caps, and high cost-sharing — their main tools for limiting substance abuse treatment spending — unless the same limits applied to other care. The bill's escape hatches (no mandate to offer the benefit, a 1% cost opt-out) limited the hit.

Large employers would have paid somewhat higher premiums for richer addiction benefits, though employers with 50 or fewer employees were exempt. Workers benefit from the coverage while sharing the premium cost.
Hospitals, residential treatment centers, and outpatient counseling providers would have gained insured patients as plans had to cover detox and rehab on equal terms.
